changes.name: Fogport Weather
changes.entry:
Fogport weather is not merely weather. Every variety is named, watched, argued over, harvested when profitable, and blamed when anything goes wrong. The condensers of the Bellworks collect, distill, refine, and sell the useful parts of the city’s fog; everyone else learns what to wear, when to stay inside, and which color means trouble.

Named Fogs

Yellowgasp

A dense yellow industrial fog, hot and metallic on the tongue, that burns the eyes and lungs of anyone not touched by the Catastrophe; goggles and aspiration masks are essential, while condenser works refine it into corrosive cleaners, stimulants, and certain medicines.

Mothfog

A rich purple fog with a deceptively sweet smell, always accompanied by clouds of Cutmoths whose blade-edged wings can flense an exposed dockhand in minutes; its distilled vapor is prized by perfumers and dye-makers.

Slackmist

Thin, bright, and ozone-scented in the morning, Slackmist gives Fogport its clearest sunlight before becoming a violent afternoon gale of rain and lightning; sailors do not set out beneath it, though stormwrights harvest its charge for spark engines.

Muld

A dull gray-brown fog with a flavor like cellar walls, Muld leaves a slick bloom of mold over roofs, ropes, food, and sleeping faces by dawn; it is rare, miserable, and valuable to brewers, tanners, and poisoners.

The Shiggins

An ordinary-looking low fog that makes barometers twitch and tempers spoil: mean men start fights, children cry at nothing, and hounds become inconsolably melancholy; weathermasters collect it in sealed bulbs for mood medicines and interrogation work.

Saltfrost

A cold white fog that leaves needles of salt on every rail, window, and beard; it preserves fish beautifully, ruins machinery, and makes every rooftop as slippery as a ship’s deck.

Sourmilk

A pale cream mist that smells faintly spoiled; milk curdles, infants sleep badly, and bakers pay well for concentrated jars used in sour breads and industrial glues.

Widowblue

A soft blue harbor fog that carries the voices of the recently dead just far enough to be mistaken for relatives calling from another street; undertakers distill it for mourning rites, while practical people stay indoors.

Gritweather

A brown, windless fog full of fine mineral dust that gets into teeth, locks, bearings, lungs, and teacups; refiners sift it for abrasives and cheap metal polish.

Toadspit

A greenish wet mist that leaves cool beads of slime on paving stones and brings toads out by the thousands; apothecaries buy the residue, children collect the toads, and nobody wears good shoes.

Mother’s Veil

A warm, pearly fog that smells of starch, soap, and old wool; it makes adults fret over absent children and makes children unusually likely to wander toward home.

Chalkmist

A dry white haze that coats everything in clean powder and makes faint handwriting appear on walls, sleeves, and faces; clerks hate it, teachers love it, and smugglers use it to reveal erased marks.

Crowfog

A black-blue mist that gathers in high places and brings flocks of wet, furious crows; their feathers are collected for fine inks, but shiny objects are rarely safe.

Cling

A clear, greasy fog that hardly seems present until coats, hair, ropes, and ceilings begin to feel tacky; it is harvested for waterproofing compounds and makes fistfights embarrassing.

Squidweather

A low pinkish fog that causes small terrestrial squids to crawl from drains, cisterns, and harbor cracks; most are harmless, but they chew leather, clog pipes, and are considered excellent eating by people from the docks.

Lungglass

A transparent fog that makes every breath feel clean and sharp until the chest begins to ache; doctors use carefully diluted Lungglass in respiratory treatments, while overexposure leaves people coughing tiny clear crystals.

Badluck Drizzle

A thin black fog that condenses into dark droplets and causes small failures: snapped laces, bad cards, dropped keys, spoiled meals, and arguments at the wrong moment; gamblers avoid it and insurers study it.

Pigeon Gray

A soft urban fog that settles only at roof height and makes birds unusually bold; pigeons gather in enormous numbers, steal food from open hands, and leave droppings used in fertilizer and war-powder.

Rustbloom

An orange mist that wakes corrosion overnight, turning old iron furry and red by morning; salvage crews curse it, foundries harvest it, and Civic Vigilance officers polish their weapons all day afterward.

Hushmilk

A thick white fog that muffles voices, footsteps, gunshots, and crying babies, though it does not stop sound entirely; smugglers adore it, ghosts are said to hate it, and mothers keep children indoors.

Greenwake

A bright green fog that leaves people alert, hungry, and unable to sleep; condenser works produce tonics from it, while dockworkers work double shifts and regret it later.

Mireglass

A wet olive-gray fog that turns the ground reflective and makes puddles look much deeper than they are; some people step around harmless water for hours, while others walk directly into canals.

Red Thread

A faint rose-colored fog that clings in strings between chimneys, railings, and fingers; textile mills collect it for dye, but lovers tangled in the same strand are said to quarrel before week’s end.

Candlefat

A yellow-white greasy mist that leaves waxy residue on lamps, windows, tools, and hair; chandlers process it into cheap emergency candles, though burning one indoors produces terrible dreams and worse smells.

The Old Salt

A heavy sea fog that arrives with no wind and tastes like wet rope, fish blood, and stone; old sailors become sentimental, young sailors become reckless, and harbor crews harvest it for brine concentrates and preservation salts.
